response: There are typically three reasons why therapy is terminated:1) Client has met therapy goals2) Client is not progressing 3) Therapist is not a good fit for clientIn order to properly assess whether therapy is helping and what progress is being made, the therapist needs to have ways of consistently checking in with clients sessions-by-session to determine what is helping, what isn't, and where the client is at in relation to their original therapy goals. When a client has met their goals, that is a good time to end counselling sessions unless the client has new goals or simply wants to check-in periodically to make sure that they are still on track (sometimes referred to as relapse prevention). When a client is not progressing, and feedback has been taken and attempts have been made to make the therapy more helpful for the client but to no avail, than it is considered unethical to continue to work with the client. In these circumstances, referring out to another therapist who may be a better fit is a good idea.

sentence: Consider seeking the help of a therapist who can guide you in identifying and addressing the root causes of your possessiveness.
response:
It's great that you're acknowledging the impact of your possessiveness on your friendships and seeking to address the underlying issues. Possessiveness often stems from deep-seated insecurities, fear of abandonment, or a lack of trust. To start working on this, consider reflecting on your past experiences, such as childhood relationships or previous traumas, that may have contributed to your possessive tendencies. Ask yourself questions like: What am I afraid of losing or happening in my relationships? What are my non-negotiables, and are they reasonable? How do I handle feelings of jealousy or insecurity?

It may also be helpful to explore the concept of attachment styles, as an insecure attachment style can contribute to possessiveness. You can try practicing self-compassion, recognizing that your worth and identity are not defined by your relationships. Additionally, work on developing healthy communication skills, such as active listening and expressing your feelings and needs in a clear, respectful manner.

Consider seeking the help of a therapist who can guide you in identifying and addressing the root causes of your possessiveness. They can help you develop strategies to manage your emotions, build trust, and foster healthier relationships. Remember that overcoming possessiveness is a process that takes time, effort, and patience, but it's worth it to nurture more fulfilling and balanced friendships.

sentence: Overcoming jealousy of your boyfriend's mother can be a challenging but ultimately rewarding process.
response:
Overcoming jealousy of your boyfriend's mother can be a challenging but ultimately rewarding process. To start, it's essential to acknowledge and accept your feelings, rather than trying to suppress or deny them. Recognize that your jealousy may stem from feelings of insecurity, fear of losing your boyfriend's attention, or concerns about his loyalty.

Consider having an open and honest conversation with your boyfriend about your feelings, using "I" statements to express your emotions and avoid blaming or accusing language. For example, "I feel uncomfortable when you spend a lot of time with your mom, as it makes me feel like I'm not important to you." This can help your boyfriend understand your perspective and reassure you of his commitment to your relationship.

It's also crucial to develop a positive and respectful relationship with his mother, if possible. Try to find common interests or activities that you can enjoy together, which can help you build a connection and reduce feelings of resentment. Additionally, set boundaries and communicate your needs to your boyfriend, such as needing quality time together or feeling included in family decisions.

Remember that his mother will always be a part of his life, and it's essential to accept and respect that. Focus on nurturing your own relationship with your boyfriend, building trust, and developing a strong sense of security and self-worth. With time, patience, and effort, you can work through your jealousy and develop a more positive and harmonious dynamic with his mother.

I had found out about a month before, but I hadn't told him I knew because I didn't want us to break up. I used to have very low self-esteem, and I think it might have to do with my dad being an alcoholic. My father cheated on my mother when I was little. I wonder if this pain has to do with that. My ex-boyfriend and I were only dating for five months, but I still can't get over this betrayal. I'm not sure what to feel to get over it: forgiveness? Hate? He helped me financially after our break up by lending me $3000, so I'm grateful for that. I still hate him for what he did and still want him to like me although we're not even talking anymore. We follow each other on Instagram and that's it. I feel like I still need his validation. This is haunting me day and night. I want to focus on my new relationship and goals, but I keep obsessing over this and keep checking my ex-boyfriend's Instagram and Facebook. I feel so bad and keep having nightmares.

sentence: What you have the chance to do now, is distinguish the reasons for your longing.
response: The dilemmas you present are giving you a great chance to understand your true reasons for being in a relationship.Continue developing some points you've written here.That you grew up sensing and/or witnessing your mom's emotional pain from your dad cheating on her, very likely set a standard in your inner self, to expect similar circumstances in your relationship life.This is a natural dynamic which happens for all of us.  What we observe in our growing up households is what we understand as "normal", no matter how bad it actually is.After all, children don't have the ability to separate that what their own parents do, is wrong compared with the rest of our culture.It is natural to long for a relationship.What you have the chance to do now, is distinguish the reasons for your longing.Is it to attach to someone who has hurt you, hasn't shown you any understanding of having hurt you, and whose validation, even if he says validating words, has little meaning because people who validate are not the ones who harm us?If you're able to teach yourself that those who love us do not harm us, and to develop new expectations for yourself of feeling good from how your partner treats you, then you will be showing yourself a road that will benefit you for your entire lifetime.
